incidents.title: Two leaders accept writes
incidents.brief: After a network blip in the orders cluster, the same order IDs are being written twice with different contents: 640 conflicts a minute and climbing.
incidents.constraint: Only one node may accept writes at a time.
incidents.question: What stops the isolated node from acting as leader?

choices.label: Require majority acks per write so the minority node can't commit
choices.resultBody: Node A cannot reach a majority, so its writes never commit and clients retry against B; the higher term makes A step down when it rejoins.

choices.label: Send heartbeats every 10 ms so failures are noticed faster
choices.resultBody: Quicker heartbeats shorten the election, but the isolated old leader still believes it leads and keeps accepting writes.

choices.label: Pick the leader as the node with the most accurate wall clock
choices.resultBody: Clock accuracy says nothing about which nodes can talk to each other; A can still keep accepting writes nobody else sees.

hints: Which side of the split has more nodes?
A write is safe only when most nodes have it.
Terms tell a stale leader to step down.

c1: 09:14:02 lost contact with B and C
09:14:05 still leader for term 7, accepting writes
c2: 09:14:04 won election for term 8 (votes: B, C)
09:14:30 order#88121 already exists with other contents
c3: replicating from leader B, lag 2 ms

culprit.explanation: Node A's log shows it committing orders with 0 of 2 follower acks while cut off: a leader in the minority kept acting alone instead of needing a majority.

wrongNodeFeedback.c2: B won a fair majority election in term 8; its conflicts come from orders A accepted on its own.
wrongNodeFeedback.c3: C is a healthy follower of B and has heard nothing from A since the blip.

incidents.title: Writes via node A time out
incidents.brief: Node A can no longer commit alone. But a third of the order clients are pinned to A and retry it for 30 s before timing out; B, the real leader, sits half idle.
incidents.constraint: Only the majority leader may commit; the partition may last minutes.
incidents.question: How do the pinned clients reach the real leader?

choices.label: Step A down when it loses majority so clients fail over
choices.resultBody: With check-quorum, A steps down within one election timeout and answers NOT_LEADER at once; client libraries try B and C and commit in milliseconds.

choices.label: Raise the client write timeout from 30 s to 90 s
choices.resultBody: A can't reach a majority however long the client waits; pinned clients now hang 90 s before the same error.

choices.label: Let A buffer writes locally and replay them to B on heal
choices.resultBody: A acknowledges orders nobody else has; on heal, replaying them collides with orders B committed in the meantime, which is the original conflict.

hints: Can A ever find out, on its own, that it lost?
A leader that can't hear a majority should stop acting like one.
Fail fast so clients try another node.

incidents.title: Four-node cluster stalls
incidents.brief: The team grew the metadata cluster from 3 to 4 nodes for safety. A 2-2 network split froze all writes for 5 minutes.
incidents.constraint: The cluster must survive any single rack failure.
incidents.question: What cluster size should they run?

choices.label: Five nodes over three racks so any rack can fail
choices.resultBody: Five nodes need three for a majority; losing any one rack of at most two nodes still leaves three, so writes continue.

choices.label: Keep four nodes and let the lowest node ID win a tie
choices.resultBody: If each half believes it holds the lowest ID, or the tie rule reads stale membership, both sides can lead; majorities exist to avoid tie rules.

choices.label: Drop to two nodes so the cluster has fewer parts to fail
choices.resultBody: A two-node cluster needs both nodes for a majority, so losing either one halts every write.

hints: How many nodes form a majority of four?
Even sizes add cost without adding tolerance.
Spread an odd count across failure domains.

incidents.title: Reads miss acknowledged writes
incidents.brief: A replicated store uses N=3, W=1, R=1. Users occasionally write a setting and read back the old value.
incidents.constraint: Reads must see the latest acknowledged write.
incidents.question: Which quorum settings guarantee that?

choices.label: Use W=2 and R=2 so every read set overlaps the write set
choices.resultBody: With R + W > N, any two replicas you read share at least one with the two that acked the write, so the newest value is always seen.

choices.label: Keep W=1 but raise R to 2 on the client's retry path
choices.resultBody: R=2 with W=1 gives R + W = 3, not more than N, so both replicas read can still miss the single replica that took the write.

choices.label: Write to all three replicas asynchronously after acking W=1
choices.resultTitle: The ack came before the copies
choices.resultBody: Async fan-out still acks after one replica, so a read that lands on another replica before the copy arrives sees the old value.

hints: When must a read set share a node with a write set?
Compare R + W with N.
Overlap guarantees you see the latest write.

incidents.title: Stale leader writes after pause
incidents.brief: A 20-second GC pause freezes the lock holder. It wakes up, still believes it holds the lease, and overwrites a file another worker now owns.
incidents.constraint: Only the current lock holder may write to storage.
incidents.question: Now what stops a paused lock holder from ever corrupting data again?

choices.label: Issue a rising fencing token and have storage reject older ones
choices.resultBody: Worker 2 got token 34 and Worker 1 still holds 33, so storage refuses the stale write even though Worker 1 thinks its lease is valid.

choices.label: Shorten the lease from 30 s to 5 s so it expires sooner
choices.resultBody: A 20 s pause outlives a 5 s lease just as easily; the paused process never gets to check that its lease expired.

nodes.sub: paused 20 s past a 5 s lease

choices.label: Have the worker re-check its lease right before each write
choices.resultTitle: The pause can hit after the check
choices.resultBody: The process can check, pass, then pause for 20 s before the write lands; only the storage side can reject it reliably.

hints: What if the process freezes between check and write?
The storage layer must be able to say no.
A monotonically increasing number orders lock holders.

mitigation.question: Worker 1 is still writing with its dead lease. What stops the damage right now?

choices.label: Kill Worker 1's process and revoke its storage credentials
choices.resultBody: With Worker 1 dead and its credentials revoked, only Worker 2 writes, and the overwritten file comes back from version history. The next long GC pause on any worker can do this again.

choices.label: Restore the overwritten file from last night's backup
choices.resultBody: Worker 1 is still running and still believes it holds the lease; its next flush overwrites the restored file within seconds.

choices.label: Scale out to three workers so Worker 2 finishes faster
choices.resultBody: The new worker takes turns on the lock correctly, but Worker 1 is still alive and still overwriting, so there is only more work for it to corrupt.

incidents.title: Fenced worker hammers storage
incidents.brief: Storage now rejects stale fencing tokens. But Worker 1 treats the rejection as a transient error and retries its write 2,000 times a second, throttling Worker 2's writes.
incidents.constraint: Fencing must stay strict; Worker 2's job must finish tonight.
incidents.question: How should a worker react to a fencing rejection?

choices.label: Treat a fencing rejection as lost lock: abort and re-acquire
choices.resultBody: Worker 1 aborts its job on the first rejection, drops its cached lease and queues for the lock again; rejects fall to zero and Worker 2's writes flow.

choices.label: Raise storage's request limit so retries don't throttle others
choices.resultBody: A higher limit lets Worker 1 retry 6,000 times a second instead; storage CPU climbs and every one of those retries is still rejected.

choices.label: Accept writes whose token is within one of the current token
choices.resultBody: Token 33 is exactly one behind 34, so Worker 1's stale write is accepted again and overwrites the file Worker 2 now owns.

hints: Can a retry ever turn a fencing rejection into a success?
Token 33 will never be valid again.
A rejected token means someone else owns the lock now.

incidents.title: Elections never settle
incidents.brief: After a leader crash, the cluster spends 40 seconds in repeated elections; candidates keep splitting the vote.
incidents.constraint: Leader failover should take a few seconds, not a minute.
incidents.question: What makes the election converge?

choices.label: Randomize election timeouts, e.g. 150-300 ms per node
choices.resultBody: Staggered timeouts let one node request votes before the others wake up, so it wins a majority on the first round and failover takes under a second.

choices.label: Give every node the same fixed election timeout for fairness
choices.resultBody: Identical timeouts are what cause the split votes: all nodes become candidates together and each votes for itself.

choices.label: Add two more nodes so a candidate is likelier to win
choices.resultBody: Extra candidates with the same timing split the vote even more ways; the fix is timing, not headcount.

hints: Why does everyone become a candidate at once?
Symmetry is the enemy of elections.
Stagger who wakes up first.

incidents.title: Leader failover lost writes
incidents.brief: The old leader acked writes after persisting locally, then crashed. The new leader never had them; 1,200 orders vanished.
incidents.constraint: An acknowledged order must survive a leader crash.
incidents.question: When should the leader acknowledge a write?

choices.label: Ack only once a majority has the entry in its log
choices.resultBody: Any future leader must win votes from a majority, and that majority overlaps the one holding the entry, so acknowledged orders survive.

choices.label: Ack after an fsync on the leader's local disk only
choices.resultBody: The entry survives on the old leader's disk, but the cluster elects a node without it and the orders never reappear.

choices.label: Ack immediately and replicate to followers in the background
choices.resultBody: A crash in the replication gap loses exactly the writes clients were told succeeded, which is how the 1,200 orders vanished.

hints: Who has the write when the leader dies?
The next leader comes from a majority.
Make the ack depend on the same majority.

incidents.title: etcd leader changes 40 times an hour
incidents.brief: KubeCo's 3-member etcd cluster runs on burstable 2-vCPU VMs with network disks. WAL fsync p99 is 180 ms, heartbeats arrive late, and the API server's p99 is 2.4 s.
incidents.constraint: The control plane must stay on etcd, and there is one maintenance window tonight.
incidents.question: What stops the leader churn?

choices.label: Move each etcd member to a larger instance with fast SSD

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Pay for dedicated cores and low-latency disks; the consensus design was never the problem.

choices.resultBody: Replacing members one at a time keeps quorum throughout. On fixed-performance instances with local SSD, fsync p99 falls from 180 ms to about 4 ms, heartbeats go out on time, and the leader stops changing. API p99 drops to 90 ms.

choices.label: Grow the cluster from three to five members for safety
choices.resultBody: Each write now needs three fsyncs instead of two on the same slow network disks, so commit latency rises. Two more slow members also mean more late heartbeats, and leader changes creep up to 45 an hour.

choices.label: Raise the election timeout to 5 s and heartbeats to 500 ms
choices.resultTitle: Holding: churn down to 6 an hour
choices.resultBody: Leader changes drop to 6 an hour and API p99 eases to 1.2 s. etcd-1's burstable CPU credit balance is falling about 8% an hour.

hints: etcd wants WAL fsync p99 well under 10 ms.
Adding members adds more of the same slow disks to every commit.
Is the problem the protocol, or the hardware it runs on?

incidents.title: etcd leader throttled at peak
incidents.brief: The 5 s timeouts held until the morning peak. etcd-1 has burned its burstable CPU credits, is throttled to its 20% baseline, misses heartbeats, and API writes time out.
incidents.constraint: The control plane must stay on etcd; members can be replaced one at a time.
incidents.question: What fixes the leader stalls for good?

choices.label: Replace members one by one with fixed-CPU, local-SSD VMs
choices.resultBody: Swapping one member at a time keeps quorum. Fixed-performance CPUs never throttle, local SSD brings fsync p99 to about 4 ms, and leader changes stop. The honest cost: about $450 a month more.

choices.label: Raise the election timeout further, from 5 s to 15 s
choices.resultBody: Fewer elections fire, but a throttled leader still stalls every commit, and a real failure would now take 15 s to fail over.

choices.label: Switch the three etcd VMs to unlimited burst credit mode
choices.resultBody: The members stop being throttled, but WAL fsync p99 is still 180 ms on network disks, so commits stay slow and API p99 sits near 2 s. Surplus credits are billed too.

hints: A credit balance hitting zero means a hard CPU cap.
Even unthrottled, the WAL waits 180 ms on every fsync.
Is the problem the protocol, or the hardware it runs on?
